messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 75, Minh Tran still speaks about the months of his son’s illness as if he is stepping back into a room he never really left. He is a widowed Vietnamese American man who has spent years working as a cybersecurity analyst, a role that suits his preference for precision and control, but when he tries to describe what happened to his child, his words start clearly and then fall apart. He can say that his son became critically ill when he was young, that there were repeated hospitalizations, procedures, and long nights under fluorescent lights, but when he gets close to the worst parts he loses the thread. He stops mid-sentence, presses his fingers together, and looks away as though the scene in front of him has become more real than the office where he is sitting.

What remains vivid are not orderly facts but sharply preserved moments. He remembers the antiseptic smell in the hospital corridors, the sting of it in the back of his throat before he even reached his son’s room. He remembers being called in while doctors prepared another procedure, seeing the equipment laid out, hearing the clipped efficiency in staff voices, and feeling a rush of fear so immediate that even now he describes it as if it is happening in the present tense. In his recollection, the memory does not feel like something concluded long ago. It returns like a film replaying on its own: the hospital bed, the small body surrounded by machines, the sense that at any second he might lose his son. What frightened him most was the helplessness of standing there as other people intervened physically in his child’s body while he could do nothing except watch and wait.

In the years since, reminders of that period have remained painfully specific. Medical examinations are especially difficult. Even routine appointments can become overwhelming once he is in a gown or hears the sounds of a clinic around him. The smell of antiseptic is enough to make his body react before he has fully registered why. His chest tightens, his hands shake, and for a few moments he is no longer an elderly man at a standard appointment but a father bracing himself for terrible news. At times he feels as though he is back in that hospital corridor, and his behavior shifts accordingly; he becomes tense, watchful, and unable to focus on what the doctor is saying. He has come to dread not just illness but the whole sensory world surrounding medical care.

Less expected to others, but perfectly coherent to him, are his reactions to babies and anything associated with pregnancy or childbirth. Seeing a newborn in a waiting room, hearing a conversation about labor, even passing an advertisement with an infant can pull him abruptly into the old terror of parenthood under threat. For Minh, babies do not simply signify happiness or family life; they immediately evoke vulnerability, dependence, and the possibility of catastrophe. He knows other people do not understand why his expression changes when a colleague shows photos of a new grandchild, but in those moments he feels ambushed by images of his own child at his most fragile.

These reactions have settled into his daily life, including at work. In cybersecurity he is respected for his concentration, but over time he has arranged his routines to reduce the chance of being caught off guard. He avoids taking assignments at hospital or healthcare client sites whenever possible, not because he cannot do the technical work, but because walking through medical buildings and catching that unmistakable hospital smell leaves him flooded and physically unsteady. He has made excuses to coworkers about scheduling conflicts rather than explain why a site visit could undo him for the rest of the day. Even in the office, a passing conversation about a birth in someone’s family can leave him staring at his screen while the old scenes begin replaying again, vivid and immediate.

He is not only frightened by the memories themselves but by the force of the emotions that arrive with them. Fear comes first, but also horror, guilt, and shame—feelings so strong that he braces against them as if they are dangerous in their own right. He is certain that if he lets himself fully enter these moments, he will be overcome. That conviction is part of why he speaks in fragments about his son’s illness and quickly turns to practical details instead. Facts feel safer than the moments he can still smell and see.

What finally brought Minh to treatment was a recent medical examination of his own. During the appointment, the odor of disinfectant and the sight of the procedure tray made him feel, suddenly and completely, that he was back beside his son’s hospital bed. He became so shaken that he could not follow the physician’s questions and had to leave before the visit was completed. The incident frightened him not only because of how intensely he reacted, but because it made him feel that all these years later the past could still take hold of him without warning. He is seeking help now because he wants some way to endure medical settings without being pulled out of the present, and because he is tired of going silent whenever he tries to tell the story that has never really become a story at all.
